claim: The debt financing the AI data-center buildout is increasingly absorbed by life insurers and the annuity accounts of ordinary Americans — and the insurers most exposed are those owned by private-equity firms. By Moody's count, U.S. life insurers' private and illiquid bond holdings grew from $685 billion (18 percent of their roughly $4 trillion fixed-income portfolio) at the end of 2024 to $807 billion at the end of 2025, a $122 billion jump in a single year. Barclays research cited in the same report put private-credit exposure above 15 percent at private-equity-affiliated insurers, including Apollo-backed Athene and KKR-backed Global Atlantic. Some of that money flows directly into AI infrastructure: Blackstone disclosed in August 2025 that its credit arm's commitments to Aligned Data Centers had passed '$1 billion and is committed entirely by accounts managed by BXCI's Infrastructure & Asset Based Credit Group' — the same unit Blackstone calls 'a leading provider of investment management services for insurers.' The chain connecting a retiree to a server farm runs through the annuity (a contract sold as safe retirement income): as a Federal Reserve research note explains, life insurers' 'funding comes from policyholders through insurance liabilities such as fixed annuities,' backed by the insurer's general-account assets — which now include this private credit and data-center debt. Regulators have flagged the build-up. The Financial Stability Board (FSB), the international body that monitors the global financial system, warned that 'a sharp correction in asset valuations, which have increased rapidly, could lead to sizeable credit losses to private credit investors,' noting the AI sector's share of private-credit deals reached 34 percent in 2025, up from an average of 17 percent over the prior five years. The Federal Reserve's November 2025 Financial Stability Report found that 'life insurers' leverage was in the upper quartile of its historical distribution.' The offshore leg compounds it: Bermuda reinsurers now hold more than $900 billion in American life and annuity liabilities, as 'insurers are seeking to transfer long-duration liabilities to reinsurers with higher-yield investment strategies, often backed by private capital.'
